name: Wild Child
beta: Starts with a 5.8 crack that transitions left through a bolted section holding the initial crux. A knee-bar rest sits below a roof; pull through onto face climbing, then a balancy sequence to an amazing finger rail, finishing with a wild romp on the left side.
overview: The crag's newest and longest single-pitch line (established Sept 2025): a mixed trad-and-bolt route starting from the Django anchors that climbs a crack into bolted face climbing with a knee-bar rest and a finger rail.

current.approach: From Highway 20, park at the pullout near Mazama before the Spires Gully parking area. Descend through trees to Early Winters Creek, cross it, follow it downstream, then angle up-slope and contour left to the crag. About 20-25 minutes. To reach the start, climb Django itself, or traverse the 'Little Squamish' bench to the Django anchors via a 5.9 finger corner or the final Django bolts.
current.descent: Route ends at a bolted/chain anchor; lower off or rappel with a single rope.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams from 0.4 to 3 inches for the opening crack, plus 12 quickdraws for the bolted upper face; bring one extendable/alpine draw.
current.pro_needs: Mixed trad (0.4-3in cams) low, bolts (12) above.

name: Wild Wild West
beta: Grade II, 5.8, fully bolted. Start at the first two bolts on a short prow at the lowest toe of the West Face. P1 climbs a short face to clean ramps to a ledge belay; P2 traverses a saddle to a chain anchor; P3 is bolted with a semi-hanging belay on a small ledge and significant exposure; P4 climbs an arete/basalt band to the summit. Pitches 3-4 are commonly combined with alpine draws.
overview: A 4-pitch bolted sport line up the lowest toe of Pinto Rock's West Face, climbing clean ramps and a cobbled rib to a saddle, then a semi-hanging belay pitch and a final pitch through a basalt band to the summit.

current.approach: From Randle, WA (Hwy 12), head south on Hwy 131, keep right and follow NF-25 for 19.2 miles. After milepost 21, turn left at the sign for Mosquito Meadows onto NF-28 and follow it for 2.7 miles, then turn left onto NF-77. Continue on this rough, high-clearance-recommended road for about 2 miles until Pinto Rock comes into view, then continue to the large pullout where the main climber's trail is clearly visible. (Alternative approach from the Portland area: I-5 north to Woodland, WA; take Exit 21 and drive WA-503 east 32.5 miles toward NF-25.) From the pullout, walk up the road toward the wall to reach the base of the West Face, or hike around via the East Face, through the gap, and drop down to the left.
approach_variant_names: Road walk from the pullout to the foot of the wall
Around the East Face and through the Gap
current.descent: From the top, descend by rappelling; head up and left along the back side of the formation near the fir trees to find the rappel anchor at the north end of the formation, which descends the East Face.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted route; carry roughly a dozen quickdraws, including several alpine draws to extend rope drag through the traverses and to allow pitches 3-4 to be combined.
current.pro_needs: Bolts protect the entire route; no natural gear is required, though a couple of long slings are useful for the traverse on P2.
current.rope_note: An exact name+grade match (5.8, 4 pitches, mostly bolt-protected, Grade II) exists on Pinto Rock's 'West Face' area: alpine draws recommended (~a dozen) to reduce drag on wandering P3/P4, rappel descent off the back near a stand of fir trees.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Most parties approach via the historic Monte Cristo townsite and the Glacier Basin Trail, then leave the maintained trail to work up talus/scree toward the col on the dividing ridge below the Wilmans Spires before gaining the northwest ridge for the final Class 4 scramble to the summit. This northwest ridge line is the peak's easiest route.
overview: The Wilmans Peaks are a cluster of two main summits and three rock spires on the ridge dividing the Monte Cristo basin from Glacier Basin, within the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness (Mount Baker–Snoqualmie National Forest). The rock is volcanic breccia; the group has no glacier and rises roughly 4,100 ft above the Monte Cristo townsite in about a mile. The neighboring East Wilmans Spire (a separate, roped alpine-rock objective, 5.6/Grade III) sits along the same ridge and is often combined with or confused for Wilmans Peak itself in trip reports — this route describes the walk-up/scramble line to the main (west) summit, not the technical spire.

current.approach: Barlow Pass Trailhead (2,362 ft) → 4 miles on the gated Monte Cristo Road to the townsite (bike-friendly) → cross the South Fork Sauk River near mile 1 via a large log or ford (no bridge — flooding destroyed the old Twin Bridges) → Glacier Basin Trail #719 toward the basin (~4,400–4,680 ft) → leave trail and scramble to the dividing ridge and the summit. The final summit block is rated Class 4 (per the 1970 first-ascent record), not a pure walk-up — expect short, exposed scrambling moves near the top, and confirm you're on the correct ridge before committing, since parties from this trailhead often end up on the neighboring East Wilmans Spire (a separate roped climb) instead.
current.descent: Reverse the Class 3-4 scramble from the summit blocks down the ridge and slopes to Glacier Basin, watching for loose rock. From the basin, follow Glacier Basin Trail #719 down to the South Fork Sauk River crossing, then the gated Monte Cristo road about 4 miles back to Barlow Pass. A bicycle left at the gate saves time on the road.
bivy: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
current.rope_note: Confirmed: Wilmans Peak (Monte Cristo area) is metamorphic volcanic breccia with a reasonable approach and no glacier travel; Class 3-4 scrambling with rockfall/loose-rock hazard.

name: South Trail / Lookout Route
beta: From the trailhead between the two Twin Lakes, the trail climbs moderately steeply through blueberry and heather slopes, meeting the High Pass Trail (#676) junction at about a quarter to half mile (stay left/straight for Winchester). It continues in tight switchbacks through fireweed and blueberries, crests a saddle/pass near 1.3 miles, then follows the final ridge to the restored 1935 lookout at the 6,521-ft summit. A short rock-cut section near the top is exposed and requires care, especially with children or dogs.
overview: Winchester Mountain is one of the most popular short hikes in the Mount Baker Wilderness, capped by a historic 1935 L-4 fire lookout that volunteers with the Mount Baker Club saved from demolition and restored in 1982; it has been open to the public for day use and first-come, first-served overnight stays ever since. The summit, reached via a steep but short trail from Twin Lakes, delivers 360-degree views across the Nooksack Cirque and Picket Range to Mount Shuksan and Mount Baker, and out to the jagged Canadian border peaks — American Border Peak, Canadian Border Peak, Mount Larrabee, The Pleiades, and Slesse Mountain — plus neighboring Tomyhoi Peak and Yellow Aster Butte.

current.approach: From the Twin Lakes trailhead (elev. ~5,200ft, parking area between the two lakes, vault toilet on site), pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest. The trail starts as a moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather slopes. At about 0.25-0.5 mile you reach the signed junction with High Pass Trail #676 (which continues on toward Gargett Mine and Mt. Larrabee views) — stay left/straight to remain on #685 for Winchester. Beyond the junction the trail breaks out of the last scattered trees onto open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs via a series of tight switchbacks through fireweed and heather, with steadily improving views back over Twin Lakes, Tomyhoi Peak, and Mt. Baker to the south. Around 0.9 mile there is an unmarked climbers'-path junction offering a more direct, rougher scramble line up snow/scree — the standard trail continues via switchbacks and is the preferred line for most parties. At roughly 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west/south of the summit; from there it's a short final push of a few hundred feet of elevation along the open ridge to the summit and the 1935 fire lookout at 6,521ft. Total distance is about 3.4-3.5 miles round trip with 1,300-1,320ft of gain, so this leg (trailhead to summit) is roughly 1.7 miles and the full gain one-way. There is no reliable water on route or at the lookout — carry all you need. The main approach hazards are: the rough final 2.5 miles of FS-3065 to the trailhead (high-clearance recommended, 4WD helpful but not required, one-lane in places), and lingering steep snow on the upper switchbacks and southeast slopes that can persist into August in heavy-snow years — an ice axe and comfort with steep snow travel is recommended for early-season ascents, since a slip on the hardened snow above the switchbacks has real consequences given the exposure below.
approach_variant_names: Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from Twin Lakes to the 1935 lookout
current.descent: This is a walk-off, not a rappel route — descend by reversing the ascent trail (Winchester Mountain Trail #685) back down the switchbacks to the High Pass Trail #676 junction and on to the Twin Lakes trailhead. No rappels are involved. The only descent-specific caution is on the upper open switchbacks and the short ridge section just below the summit/lookout, where any lingering snow patches (common into July, occasionally into August) can be firm and exposed on the downhill side — plunge-step carefully or use an ice axe if the snow is present, since this is the same terrain flagged as the trail's main hazard on the way up. Below the switchbacks the trail is straightforward and well-graded back to the trailhead.

name: Windy Peak via Iron Gate Trailhead (Boundary Trail / Sunny Pass Approach)
beta: A third option to reach Windy Peak, starting near Hodges Horse Pasture at the Iron Gate Trailhead. The line follows the Boundary Trail (#533) north to Sunny Pass, then turns west to join the Windy Peak Trail for the final approach and the same Class 2 summit scramble used by the other two routes. It involves more ascent/descent along the way than the Long Swamp or Windy Creek approaches for a similar or shorter map distance.
overview: The least-direct of the three documented approaches: a roughly 6-mile line east-southeast of the summit starting at the Iron Gate Trailhead, following the Boundary Trail to Sunny Pass before turning west onto the Windy Peak Trail network — with more elevation up-and-down than the other two approaches.

current.approach: From Loomis, take County Road #9425 north 2 miles to County Road #4066/FR-39; follow FR-39 about 14 miles, then turn onto FR-3900-500 and follow it about 6 miles (high-clearance vehicle recommended, not advised for passenger cars) to the Iron Gate Trailhead. Hike north on the Boundary Trail toward Sunny Pass.
current.descent: From the summit, retrace the Windy Peak Trail east to the Sunny Pass junction, then follow the Boundary Trail south back down to the Iron Gate Trailhead.
bivy: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows

name: Windy Peak Trail (Standard Walk-up)
beta: From Long Swamp Campground, Trail #342 climbs steadily through burned lodgepole pine to the Pasayten Wilderness boundary (~2.5 mi in), then continues through open, recovering burn and meadow to 'Two Bear Camp' (water available) and on to the Windy Peak area before the maintained tread tops out just below the true summit. The final roughly 200-300 vertical feet to the actual high point leaves the constructed trail for an easy, well-cairned Class 2 scramble over open talus/rock — the only 'technical' part of an otherwise non-technical alpine hike. Past the summit the trail continues down to join the Boundary Trail at Horseshoe Basin, so parties doing an out-and-back to just the peak should watch their turn point.
overview: Windy Peak (8,335') is the easternmost of Washington's 100 highest peaks (the "Bulgers"), standing over the remote northeastern Pasayten Wilderness about 5 miles south of the Canadian border. Unlike most Bulgers, its standard route is a non-technical trail walk-up rather than a climb — it's cataloged here for peakbagging-list completeness, and the real challenge is logistical: a long, remote approach on gravel forest roads far from any town. A gabled-roof L-4 cab fire lookout was built on the summit in 1932 by E.W. Allen and Raymond Johnson, saw brief use in the WWII Aircraft Warning Service (Jul-Sep 1942), and was removed in 1963; remnants of its old telephone line are still visible on the northwest slope.

current.approach: From Tonasket, cross the Okanogan River and drive west on Loomis-Oroville Road to Loomis. Just north of town, turn onto Toats Coulee Road (County Rd #9425, becoming #4066 then FR-39) and follow it roughly 20 miles to the junction with FR-3900-300 at Long Swamp Campground — the standard trailhead for Windy Peak Trail #342. The Windy Creek/Cathedral Driveway trailhead is about 3 miles farther west on the same road system; the separate Iron Gate trailhead is reached via a rougher spur and has the roughest driving of the three approaches (last ~6 miles).
approach_variant_names: Windy Creek trail from Cathedral Driveway
current.descent: Reverse the ascent trail (out-and-back). A loop via the Iron Gate/Horseshoe Basin trail system is possible instead of retracing the Long Swamp trail, but requires a car shuttle or significant extra road walking.
current.pro_needs: None — this is a non-technical maintained-trail walk-up. No climbing gear required.
current.rope_note: Confirmed: standard route is a Class 2 hike up the west slope via trail from Long Swamp Campground; ridge variations reach Class 3 but the standard trail route is walk-up terrain.

name: Windy Peak via Windy Creek Trail (Cathedral Driveway Approach)
beta: This alternate ('Windy Peak via the Windy Creek Trail') cuts distance versus the Long Swamp approach by starting further west/higher along Toats Coulee Road. The Windy Creek Trail climbs to meet the upper Windy Peak trail network, then shares the same final easy scramble to the true summit. The trail is clear near the first creek crossing but has accumulated blowdown further along, so expect some deadfall to step over/around in less-maintained years.
overview: A shorter, less-traveled alternate line to the same summit, starting from the Cathedral Driveway trailhead about 3 miles further along Toats Coulee Road than Long Swamp, using the Windy Creek Trail before joining the standard route for the same final Class 2 summit scramble.

current.approach: From Loomis, drive Toats Coulee Road (FR-39) roughly 22 miles to Long Swamp Campground, then continue about 3 more miles west on FR-39 to the Cathedral Driveway trailhead. The final stretch of road is gravel but reported as smooth/passenger-car friendly. In late June the road from Loomis was mostly paved and the last stretch to the trailhead was broken pavement, slow going, with a small fallen tree that drivers had to lift clear.
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the short Class 2 scramble to rejoin the trail, then descend the Windy Creek Trail back to the Cathedral Driveway trailhead — watch for the trail junction where this route splits from the Long Swamp approach.

name: Northwest Ridge (Standard Route)
beta: Wing Peak has no maintained trail. Parties approach via the Barclay Creek/Tailgunner Creek drainage to Tailgunner Pass, then climb steep snow faces and rock benches along the peak's northwest ridge. The crux is a roughly 70-degree, heavily exposed snowfinger just below the summit, above which loose Class 4 rock leads to the top. Most parties climb Wing as part of a 2-3 day traverse with Gunn Peak and Tailgunner Peak, camping near Tailgunner Pass.
overview: A remote scramble up Wing Peak's northwest ridge from Tailgunner Pass, mixing steep snow faces and rock benches with a final exposed snow/ice finger and short Class 4 summit block; almost always combined with neighboring Gunn Peak and Tailgunner Peak in the same trip.

current.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,300 ft, reached via Forest Road 6024 off US Highway 2 in Baring), follow Barclay Creek Trail 1055, then leave the maintained trail to bushwhack along Barclay Creek and up Tailgunner Creek to an old, overgrown logging road. A bootpath climbs through forest to about 4,000 ft, crosses a Class 2-3 waterfall ravine, then follows the Tailgunner Couloir (grass and snow patches) to Tailgunner Pass (roughly 5,320-5,360 ft), which lies WNW of the Wing Peak summit. A brushy spur off the forest road about 1,000 ft before the Barclay Lake lot saves roughly 300 ft of walking but is overgrown; parking on the shoulder is easier.
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb/rappel a short distance, then rappel the steepest section of the upper snow face. Below that, careful cramponing is needed through a rock defile where a narrow ribbon of snow winds between deep moats — described by one party as the most unnerving part of the descent. Continue down the northwest ridge's snow faces and benches to Tailgunner Pass, then down the Tailgunner Couloir and the bushwhack drainage back to Barclay Creek Trail and the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Parties have climbed the route with a single 30m rope, one snow picket, and about six assorted slings for protecting the snowfinger crux and building rappel anchors off the summit and upper snow face.
current.pro_needs: A light rack — a picket or two for the snowfinger crux and slings for rappel anchors (no fixed anchors reported) — plus crampons and an ice axe for the snow sections.

name: East Face Variation
beta: Begins on the line of the summer East Face for roughly two pitches, then traverses left about 30 ft with limited protection into a corner below a steep rock barrier. The crux pitch climbs this corner at about 5.8-ish with one short aid move (A0) or M5 mixed climbing to a tree belay, after which a final pitch of steep snow (using small trees for anchors) trends slightly right to finish near the summit. accounts describe the line in these general sections rather than a strict pitch-by-pitch account across all 5 rope-lengths. Rated Grade III, PG13, reflecting sustained runout climbing on marginal protection.
overview: A 5-pitch, PG13 winter mixed/ice line that follows the summer East Face for its first two pitches before breaking left onto steeper, more sustained rock/ice ground and a runout crux pitch to reach the top.

current.approach: From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100 ft, 1.5 mi north of I-90 Exit 52 via Alpental Rd), hike/skin up the main trail toward Source Lake, then turn south into the valley/basin below The Tooth's east face. In winter, avoid the summer approach path/gully directly below the East Face due to significant avalanche danger; approach via the broader basin instead.
approach_variant_names: Alpental into the basin below the east face, avoiding the summer gully in winter
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the South Face line, using its tree/gear anchors and the two bolted chain rappel stations at Pineapple Pass lower down (60m rope recommended), then hike/ski back out through the basin to Source Lake and the Alpental trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A medium winter alpine rock rack to 3 inches with doubles in the small cam sizes and extra runners/slings for the mixed and ice sections; 60m rope for the South Face rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Protection is limited on the ~30 ft traverse into the crux corner and thin through the mixed crux itself; carry doubles in small cams plus extra slings to extend runners over featured but sparsely protectable rock.

name: South Face / Standard Route
beta: This route approaches from the south after descending Aasgard Pass into the Upper Enchantments. Navigate south and southwest toward the tower's base, ascending toward the white granitic wall. Find a ledge to traverse around the east side of the tower, then scramble large black granite blocks to reach the summit. A 4-foot slot requires a jump to access the true summit. The route is exposed and requires careful footwork, especially on descent.
overview: Witches Tower is the distinct granite pinnacle at the west end of the Enchantments, about 0.4 mi east-southeast of Dragontail Peak (its nearest higher neighbor) and dividing remnants of the Snow Creek Glacier between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It's a compact, airy summit block commonly tacked on to an Aasgard Pass day, or linked with Colchuck Peak, Dragontail Peak, and Little Annapurna as part of the classic Enchantments traverse.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Mountaineer Creek Trail #1599, elev. ~3,400 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required) at the end of Icicle Creek/Eightmile Road (FR 7601), follow the trail steadily uphill through forest along Mountaineer Creek. At about 2.5 miles, bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (the right fork continues to Lake Stuart). Continue climbing, crossing a boulder-strewn section near the outlet, to reach Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly mile 4, having gained about 2,000-2,100 ft — this is the last reliable water source before Aasgard Pass. Pick up the rough climbers' path along the lake's west shore (boulder-hopping in places) to its south end, then begin the well-known Aasgard Pass climb: an unrelenting, loose boot-track/goat-trail ascent of roughly 2,200 ft in under a mile to the 7,750-7,800 ft pass. This is the crux of the approach — footing is loose scree and talus lower down, the gully sections can be wet or icy, and snow commonly lingers into July, making an ice axe (and sometimes crampons/self-arrest practice) advisable; it is also a well-documented spot for slips given the sustained steepness and long runout. From the pass, work south to southwest across talus (and often a residual snow patch) toward the base of Dragontail Peak's east side, passing the west shore of Brynhild Lake and swinging around behind Witches Tower's distinctive summit spire to its south base — the pinnacle that divides the upper Snow Creek Glacier basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. All told, trailhead to the base of the tower is on the order of 6.5-7 miles one-way with roughly 4,700-4,900 ft of gain (consistent with the ~14-mile, ~5,400 ft round-trip car-to-car days reported by parties who do this as a single push). There is significant exposure on the ledge traverse near the top, and the Enchantments are prone to fast-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer, so an early start is standard practice.
approach_variant_names: Aasgard Pass, then past Brynhild Lake and around to the south side of the tower
current.descent: Descend by reversing the scramble: back across the four-foot summit slot, down the large blocks, and around the exposed ledge to the south base of the tower. The ledge is the part to take slowly, especially if it is wet or holds snow. From the base, retrace the approach past Brynhild Lake to Aasgard Pass, then down the loose 2,200 ft gully to Colchuck Lake (plunge-step or glissade any snow with an ice axe in hand) and out on the Colchuck Lake and Stuart Lake trails to the trailhead. No rappels are needed.
bivy: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road

name: Southwest Corner
beta: From the col just southwest of the tower, ascend the sharp ridge about 100 ft, traverse a few feet right onto the South Face (Class 4), make a step-up 5.5 move, climb a short face, and scramble to the summit, jumping a 4-ft slot to reach the true top. Protection placements on the crux can be tricky to find, so an experienced leader is recommended.
overview: A short, technical variation on the standard scramble: a basic 5.5 rock climb up the sharp SW ridge and south face to the summit, best suited to parties who want a roped pitch rather than pure 3rd/4th-class scrambling.

current.approach: Same approach as the South Face route to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft), then hike south toward the tower and ascend snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of the peak (roughly 6-8 hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead).
approach_variant_names: Aasgard Pass to the col southwest of the tower
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the south face (Class 2-3) back to the col SW of the tower, then descend to Aasgard Pass and back down the loose talus/scree (or snow) to Colchuck Lake and the trailhead - roughly 1 hour from summit to the col.
current.detailed_rack: Light traditional rack for a single 5.5 pitch - small-to-medium cams and a few nuts are sufficient; leaders should be comfortable hunting for placements, which are described as hard to find.
current.pro_needs: Sparse, tricky-to-locate gear on the crux face - experienced trad leader recommended.

name: West Buttress
beta: From the col/notch behind the tower, cross a steep snowfield (ice axe recommended) to reach the base. The route climbs mostly Class 4 rock with a short Class 5 chimney partway up, on solid granite with good natural hand- and footholds, finishing with a friction-face section to the summit.
overview: An easy, two-pitch roped rock route up the tower's west side - mostly Class 4 solid granite with a short Class 5 chimney, finishing on a friction slab to the summit.

current.approach: Same approach as the other routes: Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft), then the steep Aasgard Pass trail to the col behind Witches Tower; a steep snowfield crossing (ice axe recommended) leads to the route's base on the west side.
approach_variant_names: Aasgard Pass to the col, then a steep snowfield crossing onto the west side
current.descent: Descend via a combination of rappelling and downclimbing, including a notably exposed ledge traverse, back to the col/notch; from there, downclimb the steep snowfield (self-arrest position with ice axe) back toward Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A light traditional rack suffices for two moderate pitches (small-to-medium cams and nuts); the short Class 5 chimney is the only section needing real protection.
current.pro_needs: Moderate - most of the route is unprotected Class 4 scrambling; place gear through the short chimney section.

name: With Love Lie Ancients Nestled Within
beta: One of the most popular routes at Keechelus and possibly the best 5.10 here. Features easy initial bolts followed by sustained jug hauling with a spectacular position.
overview: 5.10b/c sport route on Keechelus Ridge's East Face, featuring sustained jug climbing and described as possibly the best 5.10 at the crag with a spectacular climbing position.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive east on I-90 to Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 54, crossing to the north side of the freeway before turning onto FR 4832, then following it onto FR 4934 to the small trailhead pullout. On foot, cross the road and hike up a spur road for about 15 minutes to a flat bench, then pick up a cairned trail heading north into the forest to a rocky area, staying on the main climber's trail through a short, steeper forest section to reach the crag — roughly 25-30 minutes total from the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is generally expected for parking at national forest trailheads in this corridor.
current.descent: Single lower from the top chain anchor; at 90 ft still within a 60m rope's range.
current.pro_needs: Sport climbing route with full bolt protection.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route, 90 ft (27m), 13 bolts, chain anchor. Climbs sustained jugs; belay set from the ground (not the ledge). Standard 60m single rope more than covers it.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From the Tungsten Mine Camp junction (where Tungsten Creek Trail #534 meets Boundary Trail #533, at ~6,750 ft on the mountain's south side), follow the Boundary Trail roughly a mile west/northwest to where it bends south, then leave the trail and ascend cross-country, angling northeast up the gentle west-facing slope to the summit. Done on this line the off-trail portion is YDS Class 2; other lines/variations on the mountain may require short, low-level Class 3 scrambling. The west-slope line is reported to be the safest, least steep, and most commonly recommended way to the top.
overview: An 8,136 ft summit in the far northern Pasayten Wilderness near the Cathedral Peak area and the Canadian border. Wolframite is named for the tungsten ore mineral discovered on its slopes during the 1898-1904 US-Canada boundary survey; the historic Tungsten Mine operated on its south side from 1908-1918 (six carloads of hand-sorted ore shipped by 1920, a 30-ton shipment in 1936, and a small ore concentrator added in the early 1940s before it closed for good). The standard route is a non-technical Class 2 scramble up the mountain's broad west slopes — the real crux of the trip is the roughly 15-17 mile, 4,700+ ft one-way wilderness approach through the Chewuch River valley, making this essentially a multi-day backpack with a short scramble at the end. Peak-baggers often combine it with nearby Apex, Pope, Barchester Towers, Bauerman Ridge, Arnold, and Horseshoe Mountains on a single long Pasayten loop.

current.approach: Park at the Thirtymile Trailhead (~3,400 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road, about 29 miles north of Winthrop. From there follow the Chewuch River Trail #510 north, staying close to the Chewuch River; Chewuch Falls is a good landmark around 2.5 miles in. Around mile 8 to 8.8 the trail crosses a 2001 burn area — standing dead snags are common here and more prone to falling in wind, so be alert in storms. At roughly 8-8.8 miles (~4,700 ft) reach the signed junction with Tungsten Creek Trail #534, just after fording Horseshoe Creek, and turn right onto it. Follow Tungsten Creek Trail #534 for 6.2 miles, gaining about 2,100 ft, passing within earshot of Big Horn and Horseshoe Creeks and crossing Cinch Creek; Tungsten Creek itself, which the trail follows for its final stretch, is the last dependable water before the high country (in dry years, e.g. a September 2017 trip, sources beyond here were reported as dry streambeds and stagnant pools, so tank up). This trail ends at its junction with the Boundary Trail #533 at the historic Tungsten Mine Camp (~6,750 ft) — old mine structures, iron pipe, and building ruins from the 1908-1920s tungsten operation are visible on the south side of Wolframite Mountain. This point is roughly 14-15 miles in, effectively a full day's hike, and most parties camp near here rather than pushing to the summit and back in one day. From the mine camp junction, follow the Boundary Trail #533 west for about 1 mile to the point where the trail bends south toward Apex Pass. Leave the trail here and ascend off-trail, heading northeast up Wolframite's broad, gentle west slopes to the 8,136-8,137 ft summit; done on this line the terrain is a straightforward Class 2 talus/heather slope, though other lines or variations can involve short sections of low Class 3. This is the safest and most recommended line up the peak. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is roughly 16-17 miles with about 4,700 ft of cumulative gain, consistent with the ~34-mile (54.72 km) round trip — treat this as a backpack with a high camp near Tungsten Mine or the Boundary Trail, not a single-day car-to-car scramble. In mid-October the first 8.8 miles on the river trail are flat with few fallen trees, and the wide creek ford at the horse camp can be crossed on rocks.
approach_variant_names: Boundary Trail from Tungsten Mine Camp
current.descent: This is a walk-off with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). The standard and recommended descent reverses the ascent line: down Wolframite's west slopes (Class 2 talus/heather, with loose rock and scree underfoot — stay grouped and avoid kicking rock onto anyone below) back to the Boundary Trail #533 where it bends near Apex Pass, then east on the Boundary Trail back to the Tungsten Mine Camp junction, and finally back out via Tungsten Creek Trail #534 and the Chewuch River Trail #510 to the Thirtymile Trailhead. Parties linking Wolframite with neighboring peaks (Barchester Towers, The Pope) have also used an alternate cross-country descent off the north side: down into Wolframite's northeast basin, crossing just below a talus field, then climbing to a roughly 7,000 ft col before bushwhacking down to intersect the Boundary Trail. That variant is rougher and brushier and only makes sense as part of a multi-peak traverse; for a straightforward out-and-back, reversing the west-slope ascent route is the way to go. No fixed anchors, bolts, or technical rope work exist anywhere on this route.
current.pro_needs: Easy class 2 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
bivy: The Tungsten Creek trail camps below the Boundary Trail junction
Tungsten Mine Camp / Boundary Trail #533 junction
current.rope_note: Confirmed: western approach off Boundary Trail #533 near Apex Pass, then off-trail ascent up the gentle west side to the 8137ft summit — Class 2 if the correct line is followed.

name: Woodland Critter Christmas
beta: Follows the obvious long fingercrack layback corner on a buttress near Ellation. Chain anchor at the top. Often combined with Blood Orgy (rappel or downclimb between the two).
overview: A single-pitch fingercrack/layback corner on the buttress near Ellation, offering sustained 5.8+ crack climbing to a chain anchor; can be used as an approach/link pitch into Blood Orgy.

current.approach: This crag's coordinates correspond to the Hannegan Pass/Ruth Creek Valley area near Mt. Baker, sometimes referenced as 'Ellation Crags,' a minor, lightly-developed granite cragging/multipitch area. The general access is from I-5 Exit 255, east on SR-542 (Mt. Baker Highway) about 46 miles, then a left onto Forest Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road) for about 4 miles to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Beyond that trailhead, published approach details for the crag itself are sparse and inconsistent, so the exact on-foot route and distance are not confirmed.
current.descent: From the chain anchor atop the route, rappel ~90 ft with a single rope back to the base. Some parties instead continue directly into Blood Orgy from the top before rapping both routes. Retrace the brushy climbers' path back down to the trail and out to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Rack to 3 inches, with doubles of 0.5" and 0.75" cams recommended for the sustained fingerlock/layback crack.
current.pro_needs: Gear to 3 inches; double up on 0.5" and 0.75" sized cams for the sustained crack section.

name: Wright-Pond
beta: 4-pitch trad climbing route graded 5.11a/b (also 6c/23/VIII-/E3 in other systems). Granite climbing on Cutthroat Creek Wall. From parking, hike approximately 1/4 mile on old roadbed, look for cairns marking left turn uphill. Bushwhack through woods with no trail, gaining elevation quickly. Traverse leftward in open forest and on slabby benches to reach shoulder at base of wall's right-hand side. Expect lichen and loose rock (first climbed in 2009 and seldom repeated). Trad protection: doubles to a #3 Camalot, weighted toward small cams and wires, with RPs for thin seams. Early season may have snow/ice hazards. Rock is granite of good quality.
overview: A 4-pitch, 5.11 crack-and-corner testpiece up the previously unclimbed formation known as Little Liberty Bell, following a central left-facing arch and corner system to a treed exit near the top of the wall.

current.approach: From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 for approximately 28 miles (4.5 miles east of Washington Pass). Turn right on Forest Service Road 400 and follow for 1 mile to the trailhead parking area on the left side of the road.
current.descent: From the top, descend via 4 consecutive double-rope rappels (60m ropes) directly down the Wright-Pond line, using the bolted belays established at the P1/P2 anchors along with intermediate stations.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles to a #3 Camalot, with an emphasis on small cams and wires; RPs are noted as useful for thin seams. Bring two 60m ropes for the rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Gear-intensive corner and crack climbing throughout; small-to-mid cams (doubles to #3 Camalot) and a full range of wired stoppers cover most placements, with RPs helpful on the thinnest sections of the P1 arch/corner.
bivy: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

name: You Moss Be Joking
beta: Follows the obvious scrub line traversing left under a small roof. Pull the roof on a good crimp, step right, and walk up the slab. Belay at a large dead tree just before the hiking trail. The climbing itself is 'crappy' but it offers a way up to the upper tier with less bushwhacking than the standard walk-off.
overview: A short, easy one-pitch 5.5 that traverses under a small roof to a good crimp then eases up slab; used by some parties mainly as a lower-impact way to reach Mossy Loaf's upper tier.

current.approach: From the Barlow Pass gate, walk the closed road (old railroad grade) approximately 4 miles to the Monte Cristo townsite; a backcountry campground sits at that mark. Mossy Loaf's coordinates place it essentially at/immediately adjacent to the townsite itself, so once at the flat of Monte Cristo the formation is only a short distance further off the main townsite path. The exact final spur to the specific wall isn't well described anywhere, so on-site scouting is recommended for the last stretch.
current.descent: The route tops out at a belay beside a large dead tree just below the hiking trail; from there, walk off along the trail/wall base back to the roadside rather than descending technical ground.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack, nuts through small cams up to 2 inches; a small nut placed above the roof is worthwhile, though the climbing above is easy.
rack: Single rack, nuts through small cams to 2"
current.pro_needs: Light rack to 2 inches is sufficient; protection becomes largely optional once past the roof given the easy slab above.
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found (same unresolved 'Mossy Loaf' area as Moss Out For Harambe). Gear inferred from the easier 5.5 grade — lighter rack than its 5.7 neighbor.

name: Zool Patch
beta: Zool Patch starts up double cracks just left of Clean Break, climbs a 5.9 offwidth flake on pitch 2, then trends left on a brushy, poorly protected traverse across blank slabs (avoided rather than climbed directly) to a pair of bail trees, from which two double-rope rappels return to the base.
overview: A shorter, little-traveled 4-pitch line up double cracks and an offwidth flake 150 feet left of Clean Break on Juno Tower's east face, finishing with a brushy leftward traverse and two rappels back to the ground.

current.approach: Same approach as Clean Break: from Washington Pass, drive east on SR-20 to either the Silver Star Creek pullout (~8.5 miles) or the Wine Spires pullout (~4 miles), then hike/traverse to the east face of Juno Tower. Zool Patch starts about 150 feet left of Clean Break's start.
current.descent: From the anchors at the top of pitch 4 (double bail trees), make two consecutive double-rope rappels straight down the line of the route back to the base.
current.detailed_rack: Standard rack with hardware up to 6 inches, including gear for the pitch 2 offwidth flake.
current.pro_needs: Protection is adequate on pitches 1-2; pitch 3 crosses blank slabs described as poorly protected, which is why the route detours onto a brushy leftward traverse instead of climbing them directly.

name: The Raging Tiger
beta: Right of the big left-facing corner, work up a flake system to a stance, then carry on up the striped wall, clipping one bolt, to cold shuts below the huge roof.
overview: A mixed line on beautiful stone. A flake system leads to a stance, after which the wall above, marked with tiger stripes, is climbed with one bolt for protection to chains hidden beneath a big overhang.

name: Air Apparent
beta: Begin on jugs and follow the bolts as they slant leftward to the anchors. The direct start begins beneath a big crack inside the cave's right side, climbs buckets up and right, then powers past two bolts to merge with the regular route.
overview: A sport line on the Monolith's right flank that begins on juggy holds and slants leftward on six bolts; a harder direct start also exists.

name: Teleconnections
beta: Follow the bolted fracture until it ends, roughly thirty feet up, then shift right for a handful of moves and complete the route on the steep wall above, ending at the anchors.
overview: Follows the bolted fracture until it ends, makes a few moves rightward, then finishes straight up the steep wall. A direct start called Powertalk joins the line at the fifth clip.

name: Whip It
beta: Climb the sharp arete directly, clipping five bolts to reach the anchors.
overview: A short, sharp arete climb at a chimney that the path threads, formed by the Fern Point block against the cliff.

name: A Pocket Leaps Now
beta: Use a stick-clip for bolt one, then muscle and leap up the leaning white wall. The two neighbors end at the same lower-off and can be led or toproped for extra pump.
overview: A steep white wall route starting in a squat corner under a low roof, with two easier lines finishing at the same anchors.

beta: Start below the overlap's right end, then ascend the wall and a dihedral that faces right, reaching the toprope anchors.

name: All The Right Moves

overview: A bolted line that begins in a dihedral facing left, circles a low ceiling, and finishes with varied moves up a bulging wall.

name: Arbor Day
beta: Meander up the smooth surface right of the arete, clipping one bolt, then a pin, then two more bolts. A few nuts and small cams add security.
overview: Popular as a mixed route, it follows the smooth right-hand side of an arete, protected by bolts and a pin.

beta: Pull on the excellent holds the whole way up the corridor wall's left half to the anchors.
overview: A great route up the corridor wall's left half on excellent holds; it feels less scary than it looks.

name: Chasin' the Wind
beta: Step off a twelve-foot block, angle right past one bolt to a comfortable ledge, then run the crack until it dies and lower off.
overview: A classic two-pitch line whose second pitch is a splitter crack.

beta: Follow Smore Energy through bolt three, then cut left, passing one more bolt, to complete the climb on the arete's top half.

name: Conn's East
beta:
The first pitch works a corner toward a chockstone wedged in the primary flake, then the giant flake and chimney lead to their top, and you shift right to cold shuts.

The next pitch exits the ledge's right edge, trends right over a bulge onto good holds, and traverses about twenty feet to the anchors under Orangeaid and Alcoa Presents.
overview: A long, wandering route from 1944 that takes the easiest line across the South Peak's steep East Face, crossing many neighboring climbs as it goes.

name: Conn's East Direct
beta: Start at two shallow corners facing right, below a chockstone flake. Tricky moves gain the corners, then a widening, easier crack goes to a ledge with anchors. A brief corner and a ramp slanting right come next, then work your way back across to the left, onto the ledge under Orangeaid.
overview: A popular beginning for Conn's East that also doubles as an approach pitch to Alcoa Presents; some parties climb only the first forty feet.

name: Control
beta: Begin as Bourbon Sauce does, but at its roof head right and crank to the Kaos anchors. Then shift back to the left and complete the upper wall to the high lower-off.
overview: A variation on Bourbon Sauce that breaks right under the roof and ends at a high pair of anchors.
